newsitem.title: USA: Ohio court rules Sikh's dagger a religious object.
newsitem.headline: Ohio court rules Sikh's dagger a religious object.

text.p: An Ohio court of appeals has ruled unanimously that a Sikh was wrongfully convicted of carrying a concealed weapon because the dagger he wore was an article of religious faith in his Hindu sect.

The Ohio First District Court of Appeals on Friday overruled the conviction of the 48-year-old veterinarian, saying a Hamilton County municipal court judge acted improperly when he refused to let a jury consider religious grounds for the man's defence.
"This is basically accepted around the world, but it is not acceptable in the city of Cincinnati," the man, Dr. Harjender Singh, said on Saturday.

The turbaned, bearded Singh was charged in 1994 with carrying the weapon by Hamilton County sheriff's deputies. They found him wearing the knife, known as a kirpan in the Sikh religion, when he was detained for contempt of court in a civil case.
Appellate Judge Mark Painter said in a concurring opinion he was amazed that any judge would allow an individual's constitutional right to freedom of religion to be "trampled" in such a manner.

"What happened was ludicrous," Singh said. "The legal authorities acted like a bunch of pit bulls. The deputies, the prosecutor, the judge -- they all refused to recognise that I have any religious right to wear a kirpan."
The kirpan is worn by Sikhs to symbolise justice and honour, basic tenets to their faith, he said.
Singh, who has lived in the United States for the past 23 years, said he has not decided whether to try to recover thousands of dollars in legal expenses by filing a lawsuit against Hamilton County.
